title: The `print` statement only counts the lines that are actually displayed on the screen.
body: `print` is an operation that displays a value on the screen. Even if a value is stored in a variable, it will not appear on the screen unless you use `print`. Conversely, if there are multiple `print` statements, the output will span multiple lines. `print(x + 1)` is not code that changes the value of `x`; rather, it reads the value of `x` and displays the result of the calculation. When working on output problems, first check how many times `print` is executed and what the values inside each `print` statement are. When looking at code, focus on the execution order and the final output or return location rather than the names of the syntax elements. Intermediate calculations or variable assignments are not displayed on the screen. If there is an expression inside a `print` statement, the value calculated at that moment is printed. Since multiple `print` statements are stacked in the order they are executed, you must check how many times a `print` statement inside a conditional or loop is executed.
detail: In `print` problems, you must distinguish between what is stored in a variable and what is actually printed to the screen. Assignment operations and calculations are not visible on the screen; only the value at the moment the `print` statement is executed is printed. If a `print` statement is inside a conditional or loop statement, you must also count how many times that block is actually executed.

title: The `join` function concatenates a list of strings into a single string.
body: `join` is a method that combines multiple strings into a single string. Its syntax is not `list.join(...)`, but rather `separator_string.join(list_of_strings)`. For example, `"-".join(["a", "b", "c"])` produces `"a-b-c"`. The separator string is inserted between each element, and the result is a single string, not a list. A common mistake made by beginners is thinking of `join` as an operation that modifies a list, like `append`. `join` creates a new string result without modifying the original list. Therefore, you must store the return value in a variable—such as `result = ",".join(names)`—to use it in the next line. Additionally, the elements inside `join` must be strings by default. Attempting to use `join` directly on a list of numbers may result in an error, so you must first convert them to strings using `str` if necessary. When reading code, check three things. First, identify the separator. Second, verify that the values passed to `join` are a collection of strings. Third, check where the result is stored or output. This is particularly common in processes that assemble small pieces into a single text, such as creating filenames, merging tags, or generating a single line of CSV data. It’s helpful to think of `join` as the reverse process of `split`. `split` divides a string into a list, while `join` combines a list of strings into a single string. For example, you can use `split` to break a user-entered sentence into a list of words, then select only the necessary words and use `join` to reconstruct the sentence. If you set the delimiter to an empty string, the characters will be concatenated directly; if you set it to a space, spaces will be inserted between words. When reading the code, you should verify whether the result is printed to the screen, written to a file, or passed as an argument to another function.
detail: `join` is a function that combines a list of strings into a single string. title: Separating `return` and `print` makes functions easier to understand
body: Separating `return` and `print` makes functions easier to understand. This card is a beginner-level reading practice card designed to help you train yourself to identify the correct answer when you encounter `print` and `return` together within the same function while solving actual problems. `print` displays a value on the screen, while `return` returns a value to the caller. A function that only has `print` and no `return` may display a value on the screen, but the result of the call may be `None`. A function that only has `return` may not display anything on the screen unless `print` is called from outside, but the returned value can be stored in a variable or used in other calculations. For example, in a line like `x = make_number()`, it is more important whether the value returned by `make_number` is assigned to `x` than what is printed to the screen. Conversely, if there are multiple `print` statements inside a function, they will be executed in order, but not all of them will be treated as return values. In the case of code like `print(make_number())`—where the `print` is outside the function—the interpreter first evaluates the return value of `make_number()` and then displays that value on the screen via the outer `print`. When `print` statements inside a function and outside a function appear together, the number of printouts may also differ. This card is not meant to provide the answer immediately but rather to enhance your code reading comprehension. In function problems, screen output, variable storage, and return values are displayed separately. If you first check the execution order and the location of the final `print` or `return` statement, you’ll experience less confusion even in problems where `function`, `return`, and `print` are mixed together. When practicing, create separate columns for screen output and return values for each line of function calls. When `print` is executed, write the result in the screen output field; when `return` is executed, write the value in the field for the value returned to the calling location. Next, check whether that value is stored in a variable or passed to another `print` statement. Doing so reduces mistakes caused by mixing up the values you see with the values that are actually stored.
detail: `return` and `print` serve different purposes. `print` displays output on the screen, while `return` returns a value to the caller. If `print` statements are used both inside and outside a function, the number of times output is displayed may differ. Writing the screen output and return value in separate sections helps reduce confusion.

title: Scope is a way of distinguishing between names inside and outside a function.

body: Code preceded by `try` is executed first. If it succeeds, the `except` block is not executed.
